sections.heading: Trusting your love in every kind of day
sections.text:
Father, your love is beyond comparison. You are good when you give, and you are good when you take away. You are good when life feels bright and open, and you are good when darkness settles around me.

You loved me before I ever existed, before the world was made. In love, you rescued me through Christ. And you still love me now, even though my heart is often stubborn, ungrateful, and slow to trust you.
theological_themes: God’s goodness is not dependent on changing circumstances.
God’s electing love and redeeming grace come before and outlast the believer’s weakness.
Honest confession of hardness, ingratitude, and distrust in the presence of steadfast divine love.

scripture_references.connection: Job receives both loss and blessing under God’s sovereign hand without denying God’s worthiness. This supports the prayer’s confession that God remains good both in giving and in taking away.

Paul roots salvation in God’s love and choice before the foundation of the world, and in redemption through Christ’s blood. This directly grounds the prayer’s confidence that God loved and redeemed the believer before any merit existed.

God’s love is shown not toward the already faithful or grateful, but toward sinners through Christ’s death. That gives biblical weight to the prayer’s admission that God continues to love despite stubbornness and distrust.

sections.heading: Looking back on a year you carried me through
sections.text: Thank you for your goodness to me through another year. You have led me through a road that often felt crooked and confusing. At times I seemed to be moving backward, yet you were still teaching me, correcting me, and carrying me forward. Even when I was pushed back or weakened, you did not lose hold of me.
theological_themes: God’s providence guides the believer through confusing and difficult paths.
Setbacks and weakness can still become means of spiritual progress under God’s care.
The believer’s perseverance rests on God’s faithfulness, not personal strength.

scripture_references.connection: Moses describes Israel’s wilderness journey as a place where God humbled, tested, fed, and taught his people. This fits the prayer’s picture of being led through a twisting wilderness in ways that were painful but purposeful.

Paul teaches that God works all things together for good for those who love him and are called according to his purpose. This supports the idea that even reversals and apparent retreats can be used by God for real spiritual gain.

sections.heading: Going into the future I cannot see
sections.text:
As this year closes, I am stepping into what comes next with you. I do not know the waters ahead, and I am glad you have not shown me everything. You have been faithful in my past, and I trust you to guide my future.

So I lift the sail and pull up the anchor. Lead me, Father. I do not need to know the whole route if you are the one taking me there.
theological_themes: Faith entrusts the unknown future to God’s wise and faithful care.
God’s hiddenness about the future can itself be mercy.
The believer moves forward not by sight but by confidence in God’s presence and guidance.

scripture_references.connection: This passage calls God’s people to trust him rather than rely on their own understanding, with the promise that he will make their paths straight. It grounds the prayer’s willingness to move into an unseen future under God’s direction.
James reminds believers that they do not control tomorrow and should live under the Lord’s will. This supports the prayer’s refusal to demand advance knowledge or control over the coming year.

sections.heading: Whatever storms you appoint, keep me with you
sections.text: If you have storms of suffering for me, be with me in them. If I must face pressure, opposition, or temptation, do not let me go under. Keep me from panic, from bitterness, and from giving up. Hold me fast when I cannot hold myself steady.
theological_themes: God may allow real suffering, opposition, and temptation, yet remains present with his people in them.
The believer asks not for a pain-free life but for preserving grace within trial.
Endurance depends on God’s keeping power.

scripture_references.connection: God promises his redeemed people his presence when they pass through waters and fire. This supports the prayer’s confidence that trials may come, but God’s people will not be abandoned or finally overwhelmed.

Paul teaches that God is faithful in temptation and provides a way to endure. This grounds the request to be kept from drowning under temptation, rather than assuming the Christian can stand by personal resolve.

Paul names tribulation, distress, persecution, and danger, then insists that none of them can separate believers from the love of God in Christ. This supports the prayer’s confidence in God’s keeping love through severe trials.

sections.heading: If death comes closer, keep my faith from failing
sections.text: If this next year brings my death, then I will see your face sooner. If my ending is painful, give me the grace I will need then, not only the grace I imagine needing now. Keep my faith from collapsing. Let me finish trusting you.
theological_themes: Death is serious and painful, yet for the believer it means being with Christ.
God gives sustaining grace for the hour of suffering and death.
Persevering faith is a gift to be asked for, not a strength to presume upon.

scripture_references.connection: Paul speaks of death as gain because it means departing to be with Christ, while still valuing fruitful life in the body. This directly supports the prayer’s hope that death would mean seeing the Lord sooner.
Jesus tells Peter that he has prayed for him so that his faith may not fail. This gives biblical shape to the plea for preserving grace when suffering or death tests faith.

Christ tells Paul that his grace is sufficient and his power is made perfect in weakness. This supports asking for grace adequate to a painful end rather than pretending to possess strength in advance.

sections.heading: Use me, or set me aside, as you please
sections.text:
And if you take away work or service that I love, help me not to bargain with you. I do not get to set the terms of my usefulness. Whether my days are comfortable or hard, active or hidden, fruitful in ways I can see or only in ways you know, glorify yourself in me.

Make me the kind of person you can use whenever and however you choose. I belong to you.
theological_themes: God’s glory is the believer’s highest aim in both comfort and trial.
Christian service belongs to God; the servant does not control the form, season, or visibility of usefulness.
Surrender includes willingness to be active, hidden, fruitful, limited, or set aside according to God’s wisdom.

scripture_references.connection: Paul’s stated hope is that Christ will be honored in his body, whether by life or by death. This supports the prayer’s desire that God be glorified in either comfort or trial.
Paul uses the image of vessels set apart for honorable use, ready for every good work. This grounds the prayer’s request to be made fit for God’s use rather than insisting on a preferred role.
Paul calls believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice to God. This supports the prayer’s surrender of service, comfort, and future usefulness to the Lord.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original strongly assumes God’s providential appointment over suffering, persecution, temptation, and even the manner of death. This is a historic Reformed emphasis, but some Christian traditions would phrase God’s relation to evil and suffering more cautiously.

The line about being “cast aside from the service I love” may reflect experiences such as illness, age, removal from ministry, or loss of usefulness. I rendered it broadly as losing work or service without implying God rejects the person.
significant_interpretive_choices: I kept the nautical imagery of raising sail, pulling up anchor, and entrusting the waters ahead to God, because it is central to the original’s year-end movement into an unknown future.

I interpreted “I shall not drown” spiritually rather than as a promise of physical safety, since the original also allows for death and painful endings. The modern version asks to be kept from being finally overwhelmed or losing faith.

I rendered “chosen vessel meet always for thy use” as a surrendered desire to be made useful to God whenever and however he chooses, avoiding a claim of special status while preserving the biblical vessel imagery.
